world-93f9565596.headline: Russian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37
world-93f9565596.fulltext:
At least 37 people have been killed after a Russian drone struck a warehouse near Kyiv’s western suburbs that was storing “explosive objects”.
The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people, and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured in the strike.
More than 370 people have been evacuated from the area and the evacuation process was continuing, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said. In a statement, he said a warehouse in the town of Myla had been struck, “followed by a detonation”.
The warehouse was a depot owned by the Ukrainian military and stored shells, drones and other munitions, he said in a video address. “The first impact was on a place where ammunition was being stored that absolutely should not have been there – a depot of the defence forces. [There was] detonation of shells, mines, other munitions and drones on a significant scale,” Zelenskyy said.
Criminal proceedings had been opened on charges of official negligence, he added.
“There are regulations in place; ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas.”
He said one of the people killed was the head of the Dmytrivka community, Taras Didych, who died while rescuing others.
Ukrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into the legality of the “storage of explosive objects and materials”.
The Ukrainian prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, expressed regret that mistakes had not been learned from a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July.
An investigation into that incident, in which 22 people were killed and fires tore through nearby homes, revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations on the proximity of residential buildings.
“Unfortunately, we can already see that the terrible tragedy in Vyshneve did not become a lesson,” Koretskyi said. “In the fifth year of a full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes is criminal negligence. And all those guilty, without exception, must be severely punished so that such situations do not happen again.”
In a statement, Russia’s ministry of defence said it had hit a warehouse in Myla storing components and launch boosters for long-range drones. It said it had also attacked the ports of Mykolaiv and Izmail, as well as a logistics centre and warehouse facilities storing parts for Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles in the Kyiv region.
Elsewhere, Russian attacks across Ukraine’s southern Kherson region killed two people and wounded 27 more on Saturday, including a child, a local official said.

other-interests-12c58e4fa2.headline: Praggnanandhaa becomes first Indian to win Grand Chess Tour title
other-interests-12c58e4fa2.fulltext:
He was trailing. And he was up against the World No. 2. And yet, there was almost a sense of inevitability to it. R. Praggnanandhaa duly defeated Fabiano Caruana and won the Grand Chess Tour.
After losing the first game, he bounced back in great style to win the multi-format final at St. Louis on Thursday (August 27, 2026). He became the first Indian to win the most prestigious tour on the chess circuit.
Caruana, in fact, was the champion of the Grand Chess Tour last year, and also in 2023. He had begun on the right note in the U.S. city, winning the opening classical game of the final against his 21-year-old rival from Chennai, whose blunder with his rook on the 28th move proved fatal.
Praggnanandhaa, however, came back strongly in the second classical game, in which he was in control before an error of judgment allowed his American opponent to draw after 95 moves. Caruana thus maintained his lead, 9-3 (a classical win carried six points).
The Indian, however, showed his supremacy in the faster time controls. He won both the rapid games — worth four points each — and thus took an 11-9 lead going into the blitz section. Caruana was in a must-win situation in the last blitz game, but Praggnanandhaa drew it with perpetual checks, giving him a 15-13 match victory.
He is indeed looking unstoppable on the chessboard. This is his second major success at St. Louis this month. Just a fortnight ago, he had won the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz in spectacular style. He won the tournament by a margin of 1.5 points, over his nearest rival Javokhir Sindarov, this year’s World championship challenger. Praggnanandhaa was leading on all five days of the event.
Before Saint Louis, he had recorded a career-best performance at Norway Chess in Oslo, where he emerged as the champion after beating the World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen twice in his hometown. The five-time World champion has often spoken highly of him and once even named him as the player closest to him in style.
That is indeed high praise. Pravin Thipsay, India’s third Grandmaster, believes Praggnanandhaa has earned it. “He has a great sense of what is required to win, and it is not about a better position or a complex position,” Thipsay tells The Hindu over the phone from Mumbai. “He has a knack of where that initiative is and goes for non-simplification like Carlsen. And he goes beyond the book and is a very active player even when the positions are equal. He has become a very strong player practically.”
Praggnanandhaa’s recent successes have come after he went through one of the worst periods of his career. He was so badly out of form in the year’s most crucial event – the Candidates tournament in Cyprus, where he was placed seventh in a field of eight.
If he continues to play like this, he could be one of the favourites for the next Candidates. “Yes, he will be a great force,” says Thipsay.

other-interests-a13cd710d1.headline: Siraya language, deemed ‘extinct’ over a century ago, finds its voice again in Taiwan
other-interests-a13cd710d1.fulltext:
- A family of Siraya activists in Taiwan is a major driving force behind the revival of their ancestral language — more than a hundred years after it was last spoken.
- The work to revitalize the Siraya language, which began more than 20 years ago, helped secure the community’s legal recognition as Taiwan’s 17th Indigenous group.
- The story of the Siraya language’s revitalization began as a love story between Siraya activist Uma Talavan and Filipino musician Edgar Macapili.
- While she could not understand a Dutch missionary’s Siraya translation of the Gospel of Matthew, her husband recognized similarities between the Siraya language and his mother tongue, Bisaya, both of which belong to the Austronesian language family.
TAINAN, Taiwan — Since she was old enough to understand it, Uma Talavan has known she belongs to the Indigenous Siraya people.
She knew almost nothing of her ethnicity, however, the identity of which was dissolved by centuries of forced assimilation, save for a handful of words her parents used to speak. In search of “who she is,” as she puts it, the Siraya activist decided to bring her language back to life nearly 200 years after it died out.
“Language is an extremely important part of a people’s soul,” she says. “It lets us know the past and connect it to the present.”
Her work to revitalize the Siraya language, which began more than 20 years ago, helped secure the community’s legal recognition as Taiwan’s 17th Indigenous group. Uma Talavan, her activist father Wan Cheng-hsiung, also known as Cheng-hiong Talavan, and other members of the community traveled from Tainan to Taipei to attend a ceremony announcing the recognition on July 30.
The Siraya, one of Taiwan’s Austronesian-speaking Indigenous peoples, are the largest of the Pingpu groups, the peoples who have traditionally inhabited the island’s lowland plains and coastal areas. When the Dutch arrived in southern Taiwan in the 17th century, the Siraya were the first people they came into contact with.
The story of the Siraya language’s revival begins as a love story. In 1992, Uma Talavan met her future husband, Edgar Macapili, during a stay in the Philippines. Both musicians, they grew close playing music together at a local church. After settling in Taiwan, Macapili wanted to help his wife reclaim her lost identity.
Uma Talavan and her father got hold of a copy of the Gospel of Matthew translated into Siraya by a Dutch missionary during the Dutch colonial period from 1624 to 1662.
When she showed it to her husband, they had a breakthrough: He recognized similarities between the Siraya language and his mother tongue, Bisaya, an Austronesian language spoken in the central and southern Philippines.
“We felt like we were witnessing a miracle,” Uma Talavan, 62, tells Mongabay in a classroom at Koupi Experimental Elementary School, the first school where learning Siraya is mandatory, in Tainan, a city in southern Taiwan.
Her 63-year-old husband nods in agreement.
“We deciphered every word of the religious text one by one and translated them into English, then we published the first Siraya dictionary in 2008,” Macapili says.
“As a composer, I took the Siraya texts and set them to music. Children learned Siraya that way, by singing. We wrote songs to teach counting, for instance, and we scaled up that teaching method.”
According to Uma Talavan, 45 teachers, all trained by her and her husband, currently teach Siraya at 26 schools across Taiwan. Activists hope the legal recognition will help them access more state support to develop the language.
For the pioneering family, the recognition of the Siraya and the revival of its language is a story of generational transmission.
“It’s a very young language, and for now it’s mostly spoken by children; it isn’t yet used in daily life,” says Lici Talavan, the couple’s younger daughter.
The 28-year-old has become a Siraya-language teacher, a job she juggles alongside her anthropology studies at Tsing Hua University in Taipei.
Lici Talavan says that her elder sister, Euphony Talavan, has spoken to her children in Siraya since they were babies. “They speak it better than I do now,” the proud aunt adds, noting that “they are the first generation to speak revitalized Siraya” from birth.
Beyond academia
The study of Siraya used to be confined only to academic research. “Researchers weren’t interested in revitalizing the language,” Lici Talavan says. “That was a path our family chose to take, becoming Siraya people who speak Siraya.”
Karl Alexander Sander Adelaar, a linguist specializing in Austronesian languages, concurs. “There was criticism from Taiwanese academia,” says Adelaar, who is an honorary principal fellow at the University of Melbourne’s Asia Institute. “Researchers saw the revitalization of Siraya as a big joke.”
He was involved in reviving the language after he received an email from Macapili in the 2000s, asking for his help. Although convinced the Indigenous language was doomed to be forgotten, he says, the Dutch linguist traveled to Taiwan.
“I knew Siraya people had once lived around Tainan, but I thought they’d all become Chinese, and that anyone who remembered having Siraya ancestors probably wouldn’t want to talk about it,” Adelaar tells Mongabay.
Under the Qing dynasty, Japanese rule and the Kuomintang regime, Pingpu Indigenous communities, including the Siraya, were coerced and pushed to assimilate far more forcefully than their highland counterparts. Because of this, the Pingpu people were considered not “Indigenous” enough to qualify for official status.
The use of the Siraya language declined, with linguists considering it “extinct”, meaning no native speakers, by the 19th century. Siraya activists, however, prefer to call it “dormant”.
Adelaar says he remembers how emotional the Siraya people were when they witnessed the fruit of their language revival.
“When Edgar Macapili invited me to present a 100-page Siraya grammar book to the community, people started crying,” he says. “These were people who’d had their past taken from them, and suddenly, there was a book. Suddenly, they had a history, and it had been given back its dignity. That kind of weeping is something I never expected to witness.”
Because a language’s phonology can’t be reconstructed from written texts alone, the revitalized Siraya of the present is not the same as the Siraya of centuries past. However, the academic says he believes this isn’t important.
“The language can’t be resurrected 100%, because you don’t even know how it was spoken hundreds of years ago,” Adelaar says. “What matters most is the emotion, the sense of belonging, and the soul of a community rediscovered.”
Teaching language to parents
In October 2022 — 12 years after Uma Talavan filed an administrative lawsuit — Taiwan’s Constitutional Court issued a landmark ruling, paving the way for the Siraya and other Pingpu groups to be officially recognized as Indigenous.
Among the arguments presented to the top court was the Siraya’s linguistic revitalization work, which activists believed helped convince the justices to rule in their favor.
In October 2025, lawmakers finally passed the Pingpu Indigenous Peoples Status Act, and nine months later, the cabinet conferred official status on the Siraya.
Since Aug. 13, Siraya people have been able to apply to register as Indigenous, a process undertaken by Uma Talavan and her family. There is no official data on how many people of Siraya descent are in Taiwan. But the Tainan city government, long supportive of their legal fight, recorded more than 11,800 people as Siraya in 2016.
To register as Indigenous, Silia Pan, a Siraya-language teacher at the 106-year-old Koupi School, had to trace her lineage back to Japanese colonial rule between 1895 and 1945.
In household registries from that era, the Siraya were classified as shú (cooked), a category adopted from the Qing dynasty that was applied primarily to lowland Indigenous populations considered “assimilated”. If the residence recorded at the time matches one of the sites now recognized as former Siraya settlements, that combination of factors is enough to file a claim for recognition as Indigenous.
“I’m proud to have fought to be recognized and taken into account by the state,” says 54-year-old Silia Pan, who recently made an application to register as Siraya.
After learning Siraya from Uma Talavan and Macapili, she says she taught it to her son and her father.
“It’s something quite extraordinary that this is happening in our time: Children teaching their language to their parents,” she says. “We’re learning the language of our ancestors together, and it brings us closer.”

While Yash’s performance and the film’s visuals have received praise, its screenplay and storytelling have drawn mixed reactions.
The film has nevertheless opened strongly at the box office, crossing ₹200 crore worldwide within its first three days.
The mixed response to Toxic comes at a time when the Indian film industry is witnessing a strong box-office year overall.
The first half of 2026 has proved to be the strongest post-pandemic period for the Indian box office.
According to an Ormax report, films released between January and June collected ₹6,398 crore at the box office.
This is ₹650 crore more than the collection during the first half of 2025.
2026 could also set a new record in terms of overall earnings.
Over the past three years, January-June collections have accounted for an average of around 42% of the full-year box office revenue.
If the same pattern continues in 2026, the ₹6,398 crore earned in the first half could translate into annual box office collections of around ₹15,200 crore.
This means the Indian box office could cross the ₹15,000 crore mark for the first time.
Last year’s ₹13,395 crore record could be broken
The Indian box office recorded an all-time high collection of ₹13,395 crore last year. Based on the first-half trend, 2026 could go beyond that figure.
The second half of the year also has several major releases lined up, which could further boost overall collections.
Hindi films strengthen their hold, while Tamil films’ share declines
Hindi cinema has increased its share of the Indian box office during the first half of 2026.
The box office share of Hindi films increased from 39% to 44%.
Tamil films’ share fell from 17% to 12%.
Marathi films recorded a 4% share, their highest level since the pandemic.
South Indian films continued to perform strongly among the top 10. Four of the top 10 films were Hindi-language releases, while six were from South India.
The figures show that while Hindi films have strengthened their position, films from the southern industries continue to make a major contribution to the overall Indian box office.
₹200 crore club grows, but ₹100 crore club shrinks
The number of films crossing the ₹200 crore mark has increased in the first half of 2026. Six films crossed ₹200 crore, compared with four during the same period in 2025.
However, the ₹100 crore club saw a decline. As many as 17 films had crossed ₹100 crore between January and June 2025, while the number fell to 13 in the same period this year.
This indicates that while the biggest films are earning more, the number of mid-level films reaching the ₹100 crore mark has reduced.
Theatre footfalls also show strong growth
The box office growth is not limited to collections. Theatres recorded 37.8 crore footfalls in the first half of 2026, around 5% higher than the 36.2 crore recorded during the same period in 2025.
After the pandemic, the annual record stood at 94.3 crore footfalls in 2023. With 37.8 crore footfalls already recorded in the first six months of 2026, the industry could potentially set another major record by the end of the year.
Big releases in the second half could push the numbers higher
The second half of 2026 has several major releases lined up, including Ramayana: Part 1, King and Avengers: Doomsday.
These films are expected to bring more audiences to theatres and could play an important role in pushing the annual footfall figure higher.
If the current trend continues and these major releases perform well, the Indian theatrical market could cross the 100 crore footfall mark by the end of 2026.
Overall, the year has presented an interesting picture for Indian cinema. While films such as Toxic are facing mixed audience reactions despite strong initial interest, the wider box office is showing healthy growth.
With ₹6,398 crore already collected in the first half, 2026 is on course to potentially become the biggest year in the history of the Indian box office.
One important editorial point: I would avoid writing that Toxic is simply “not getting views” or “not getting audience response” because the available reports show a mixed reception but strong opening/early collections.
That distinction makes the article more accurate and stronger journalistically.

Crashfree India Call for Applications: Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) Cohort 2026–27
Crashfree India is accepting applications for the Cause Marketing Fellow position under its Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship (SMIF) Cohort 2026–27. The full-time fellowship offers an opportunity for graduates and early-career professionals to contribute directly to road safety and safer mobility initiatives across India.
Based in Gurugram at the Cars24 headquarters, the fellowship runs for one year and provides a monthly fellowship allowance of ₹50,000. The programme is designed as an immersive professional placement rather than a conventional academic fellowship, giving participants responsibility for meaningful projects and exposure to government institutions, civic authorities, researchers and other stakeholders.
About the Fellowship
The Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship focuses on one of India’s most pressing public challenges: road safety and safer mobility. Fellows are expected to work closely with experienced teams, take ownership of defined workstreams and contribute to projects intended to generate measurable real-world impact.
The programme places strong emphasis on execution, accountability, problem-solving and leadership. Rather than simply observing existing programmes, fellows are expected to contribute to designing, implementing and improving initiatives.
The Cause Marketing Fellow track is currently open for applications for the 2026–27 cohort, while other fellowship tracks have closed after receiving sufficient applications.
Fellowship Details
Position: Cause Marketing Fellow
Programme: Safer Mobility Impact Fellowship
Cohort: 2026–27
Location: Gurugram, India
Workplace: Cars24 Headquarters
Duration: One year
Schedule: Full time
Monthly allowance: ₹50,000
Eligibility: Graduates and early professionals
Current track: Cause Marketing Fellow
Who Should Apply?
Crashfree India is seeking individuals who demonstrate initiative, ownership and a genuine interest in solving complex public challenges.
The fellowship is particularly suited to candidates who are comfortable working in ambiguous and high-accountability environments. Successful fellows are expected to make decisions, move projects forward and focus on measurable outcomes rather than simply contributing to discussions.
Candidates should have a genuine interest in road safety, urban systems, evidence-based policy or related public-interest issues. Strong communication, problem-solving and execution capabilities are also important.
The programme values demonstrated potential and the ability to deliver over credentials alone.
Cause Marketing Fellow Role
The Cause Marketing Fellow will contribute to Crashfree India’s efforts to build awareness, engagement and support around road safety initiatives.
The role provides an opportunity to work on communications and cause-marketing activities connected to major road safety programmes. Depending on organisational priorities, responsibilities may involve campaign development, stakeholder engagement, content and communications, public outreach and efforts to increase the reach and visibility of road safety initiatives.
The fellow will be expected to take ownership of assigned projects and work closely with internal teams and external stakeholders.
Selection Process
The fellowship selection process consists of five stages designed to evaluate problem-solving ability, communication, ownership and alignment with the organisation’s mission.
Step 1 – Registration: Candidates submit basic information and a résumé and indicate their preferred fellowship track.
Step 2 – Assignment: Applicants complete a short assignment relevant to the selected role. The exercise assesses problem-solving, communication, ownership and execution thinking.
Step 3 – Round 1 Interview: Candidates participate in a skills and capability assessment focused on how they structure and approach problems under conditions of ambiguity.
Step 4 – Round 2 Interview: The second interview focuses on mission alignment, culture and the candidate’s commitment to the road safety cause.
Step 5 – Fellowship Start: Selected fellows begin their placement at the Cars24 headquarters in Gurugram.
What Fellows Gain
The programme is designed to provide professional experience through direct involvement in real projects.
Fellows receive expert mentorship from senior practitioners and academic experts, with guidance connected directly to their work and deliverables.
Participants also gain external stakeholder exposure, including opportunities to engage with government bodies, civic authorities and institutional partners as professionals rather than observers.
The fellowship also provides experience in leadership and programme ownership, with fellows expected to manage workstreams, timelines, stakeholders and other components of project execution.
Previous Fellowship Impact
Crashfree India highlights several outcomes generated by its inaugural fellowship cohort. These include Project Rakshak, a youth-led road safety audit initiative that assessed high-risk locations across India and secured civic authority approval for infrastructure interventions.
Another initiative, the NextMile Ideathon, generated more than 250 policy submissions addressing gig rider safety and crash claim compensation. Shortlisted proposals were formally submitted to the Government of India.
The fellowship also supported research into gig worker safety and post-crash legal challenges, involving hundreds of stakeholder and worker interactions and engagement with government ministries.
These examples demonstrate the programme’s emphasis on moving from research and analysis to practical implementation, policy engagement and public impact.
Career Development
The fellowship offers participants an opportunity to develop career capital through substantial professional responsibilities. Fellows can strengthen their experience in cause marketing, communications, stakeholder engagement, public policy, research, programme management and social-impact initiatives.
Participants may also develop professional networks through engagement with government agencies, civic institutions, academic experts, private-sector organisations and other road safety stakeholders.
How to Apply
Candidates interested in the Cause Marketing Fellow position should submit their application through Crashfree India’s official fellowship application process. The organisation encourages prospective applicants to review the role carefully and demonstrate their ability to take ownership of consequential projects.
Questions about the fellowship can be directed to [email protected].
The opportunity is particularly relevant for graduates and early-career professionals seeking a demanding, hands-on experience in road safety, cause marketing, public-interest communications and social impact.
